section.title: Applications of Taylor series
section.p: The last section collected Taylor series for the elementary functions:
These formulas are not only identities. They are tools.

A Taylor series can turn a difficult function into a polynomial calculation. That makes it useful for estimating function values, evaluating limits, approximating integrals, and solving differential equations.
section.md: \text{A Taylor approximation is useful only when its error is controlled.}
section.p: So every application in this section will keep the error visible.

A Taylor series is local information. A good computation respects that locality.

exercise.title: Why should a Taylor computation respect locality?

statement.p: To estimate e^{3.02}, it is better to use a known value of e^3 and expand only e^{0.02}. In your own words, why do Taylor series work best near their center, and what strategy does that suggest for logarithms and trigonometric functions as well?

hint.p: Powers of a small remainder shrink quickly, and the remainder bound is controlled by distance from the center. Move the hard part into a known value; let Taylor work on a nearby leftover. Use radians for sine and cosine.

subsection.title: Evaluating limits
subsection.p: Taylor series are especially powerful for limits where direct substitution gives
They reveal which terms cancel and which term survives.

exercise.title: Why can Taylor series evaluate a limit that looks like cancellation?

statement.p: A limit that pits two functions against each other often asks which derivative first distinguishes them. In your own words, why do you keep Taylor terms until the first surviving term after cancellation, and why is that still the derivative story in disguise?

hint.p: Matching initial derivatives makes the first few terms cancel. The first unmatched term is the first local difference, which is exactly what a higher derivative measures.

statement.p: As x\to0, every remaining term with a positive power of x goes to 0. Therefore
The series showed the true leading behavior:
The constant and linear terms cancel. The quadratic term is the first surviving term.
Here the first two nonzero Taylor terms of \ln(1+x) were not enough. They canceled with the expression in the numerator. We had to keep the first term that survived.

note.title: Taylor limit strategy
note.p: To evaluate a limit using Taylor series:

li.p: Expand each function around the point of approach.
Keep enough terms to see the first nonzero term after cancellation.

statement.p: This method is not separate from the derivative story. Taylor series are built from derivatives. A limit that asks about cancellation is often asking which derivative first distinguishes two functions.

exercise.title: Why can a series approximate an integral with no elementary antiderivative?

statement.p: The integrand e^{-x^2} has no elementary antiderivative, yet its Taylor series can be integrated term by term. In your own words, why does replacing a function by a polynomial near the center turn a hard integral into arithmetic, and why must the remainder still be watched?

hint.p: Polynomials are easy to integrate. The series is justified on an interval inside the radius, so the integrated tail is a boundable error rather than an unknown mystery.

subsection.title: Solving differential equations by series
subsection.p: A differential equation gives a law for an unknown function. Sometimes the solution is one of the familiar functions. Sometimes it is not.
Power series give a way to build a solution from its coefficients.
The idea is to assume
substitute into the differential equation, and match coefficients.

exercise.title: Why can a differential equation be solved by matching coefficients?

statement.p: Assuming y=\sum a_n x^n and substituting into a differential equation produces relations among the coefficients. In your own words, why is that a way to build a solution from local data, and why must an application still report an error bound rather than a polynomial alone?

hint.p: A differential equation is a law for derivatives. A power series stores those derivatives as coefficients. The resulting algorithm is trustworthy only when the leftover terms are controlled.

subsection.title: Error bounds in applications
subsection.p: In applications, an approximation is judged by the error the situation can tolerate.
A navigation problem, a physics simulation, and a classroom estimate may all use the same Taylor series, but they may require different numbers of terms.

paragraphs.p: Taylor series turn functions into algorithms. But the algorithms work because their errors can be bounded. The next section explains, in a preview form, why power series allow such safe term-by-term work inside their radius of convergence.
